newsitem.title: UK: Time to shine for precious metals' Cinderella.
newsitem.headline: Time to shine for precious metals' Cinderella.

text.p: Palladium, at a record high official price on Wednesday, is the humblest of the precious metals.
Most of it's hidden away in dental work or car exhaust sytems.

And only rarely does it emerge from the shadow of more glamorous gold, silver and platinum - its sister rare white metal - as it did, for instance, in 1989, when it was used in experiments that briefly seemed to herald a new energy source in "Cold Fusion".
Prices soared on Wednesday on news of a strike at Rustenburg, the world's largest platinum mine, in South Africa that followed five months of delay in exports by Russia, the biggest supplier.
Palladium was fixed in London at $188.00 an ounce, its highest ever official setting. Platinum, at $404.50, matched its recent highest fix nine months ago on August 1, 1996.
As recently as the end of last year, palladium was at a more normal price below $115.
"It takes really something special for palladium to be at over $180," one precious metals market analyst said.
Platinum group metals are used in electronics, chemical applications and autocatalysts which remove noxious gases from car exhausts.
But whereas platinum is a favourite among jewellers, palladium is otherwise chiefly used in making dental alloys.
A handful of producers in South Africa and Russia dominate supply to the markets of which Japan is the largest.

Trading in these metals has always been a low key business compared to that in gold. Gold has been hoarded by governments and individuals as a store of value for centuries, so that almost every tonne of it ever mined is still being stored somewhere on the planet.
But platinum and palladium have always gone straight to industry or jewellery, except for a small tonnage held mainly in Japan where investors buy platinum bars.
They only became "official" markets in London in 1989, which was 70 years after the gold market established its price "fixing" process.

The current fixing provides a twice-daily reference point on which pricing for contracts can be based. It represents the matching of orders from customers around the world so that dealers, investors, miners and consumers can buy and sell at a price which satisfies all current interest.

The rare white metals soared at the end of the 1970s, when gold and silver reached historic highs on fears of inflation, after the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries lifted the cost of oil to $40 a barrel.
Platinum reached its highest unofficial value at around $1,050 in early March 1980 and palladium peaked at around $335.00.

Since the official fixings began, palladium's top price was $181.50 in 1989 when laboratory tests suggested that "Cold Fusion" might work, creating a new demand for the metal. But the price collapsed when further reasearch failed to stand up initial results.
In April 1995 another new application for palladium was briefly in the spotlight and prices raced again.

The Engelhard Corporation announced its Premair "revolutionary clear air catalyst system" with potential to reduce ground-level ozone and carbon monoxide throughout the world. The price reached $178.50 on April 5 but a month later it was worth $20 less as news about Premair dried up.
